question.question:
D1 — Rebuild retry scheduling, or drive the library's retry hook with a custom curve?
Project/branch/task: main — plan "Add background job retry framework", PLAN.md:7-9.
ELI10: The job library you already run has a retry hook. The plan rewrites that machinery by hand inside every worker, admitting it is the "same shape as the library version", purely to own the delay curve. Most job libraries let you plug in your own delay function, so you can usually get full control over the curve without rebuilding attempt counting, max-attempt cutoffs, dead-lettering and crash recovery.
Stakes if we pick wrong: a hand-rolled scheduler that loses the attempt counter on a crash either retries forever or drops the job silently, and five copies means five places to get it wrong.
Recommendation: A because the plan states no behavioral difference from the library version, and a custom backoff function inside the library hook gives the same curve control with the library's persistence and cutoffs intact. [Layer 1: reuse the installed dependency]
Completeness: A=10/10, B=4/10, C=n/a (investigation only, approves nothing)
Pros / cons:
A) Library retry hook + custom backoff function (recommended) (human: ~1 day / CC: ~20 min)
  ✅ Keeps the library's attempt persistence, max-attempt cutoff and dead-letter handling, which the plan would otherwise have to reimplement
  ✅ Full control of the delay curve lives in one small pure function that is trivial to unit test
  ❌ Must confirm the installed library version exposes a custom delay callback; if it does not, the curve may need an upgrade or a thin adapter
B) Custom inline scheduler per worker (as proposed) (human: ~1 week + ongoing / CC: ~2 h + ongoing)
  ✅ Zero dependence on the library's hook semantics or version
  ✅ Curve, logging and dispatch can be tuned per worker independently
  ❌ Reimplements attempt counting, cutoffs, dead-lettering, jitter and crash-mid-retry handling that the library already provides, and does so five times
C) Investigate first: bounded probe of the library's hook API (human: ~1 h / CC: ~5 min)
  ✅ Settles the one open fact (does the hook accept a custom delay function?) before committing
  ✅ Costs almost nothing and leaves every other choice untouched
  ❌ Approves no implementation; R1 stays pending until the probe result comes back

question.question:
D2 — When webhooks start retrying, what delivery guarantee do receivers get?
Project/branch/task: main — plan "Add background job retry framework", PLAN.md:17-19.
ELI10: Today a webhook is sent at most once: if it fails, it is gone, but the receiver never sees a duplicate. Adding retries flips that. A send that timed out may have actually landed, so the retry delivers the same event twice. Receivers that charge a card or create a record on each webhook will do it twice. The standard fix is an idempotency key: a stable id per delivery that goes out with every attempt, plus a record on our side so a retry never re-sends something already confirmed.
Stakes if we pick wrong: duplicate webhooks cause double side effects at every customer endpoint, and nobody on our side sees an error.
Recommendation: A because retries on webhooks are only safe when receivers can dedupe, and the key plus delivery record is a small addition that turns the silent-duplicate failure into a defined contract. [Layer 1: standard webhook practice]
Completeness: A=10/10, B=7/10, C=3/10
Pros / cons:
A) At-least-once with idempotency key + delivery record (recommended) (human: ~2 days / CC: ~30 min)
  ✅ Receivers can dedupe on a stable id; the contract becomes explicit and documentable
  ✅ A persisted delivery record stops a retry from re-sending an attempt that already succeeded
  ❌ Adds a small write per attempt and a schema change for the delivery record
B) Keep retries off for processWebhookJob (human: ~1 h / CC: ~5 min)
  ✅ Preserves today's at-most-once guarantee with no receiver-facing change
  ✅ Smallest possible change to the webhook path
  ❌ Failed webhooks are still dropped silently, which is the pain this plan exists to fix
C) Retries on, no idempotency key (as proposed) (human: ~0 / CC: ~0)
  ✅ No extra schema or header work
  ✅ Ships fastest
  ❌ Receivers get duplicate deliveries with no way to detect them; double side effects at customer endpoints
Net: a small id plus one table row per delivery versus silently duplicating customer-visible side effects.

options.label: At-least-once + idempotency key (recommended)
options.description: Enable retries on processWebhookJob through the library hook (R1). Send a stable per-delivery idempotency id on every attempt, persist a delivery record and check it before each send so a confirmed attempt is never re-sent. Completeness 10/10. Effort human ~2 days / CC ~30 min. R2-R5 stay pending; R3's regression contract will target this guarantee.

options.label: Retries off for webhooks only
options.description: Keep processWebhookJob at-most-once with no retries; the other 4 workers get retries via R1. Failed webhooks remain dropped. Completeness 7/10. Effort human ~1 h / CC ~5 min. R2-R5 stay pending; R3's regression contract will target at-most-once.

options.label: Retries on, no idempotency (as planned)
options.description: Enable retries on processWebhookJob with no idempotency key or delivery record. Receivers may receive duplicates. Completeness 3/10. Effort none beyond R1. R2-R5 stay pending; R3's regression contract will have to document the duplicate-delivery behavior.

question.question:
D3 — Should the backoff curve add random jitter?
Project/branch/task: main — plan "Add background job retry framework", PLAN.md:7-9.
ELI10: When a downstream service goes down, every job that touches it fails in the same second. With a pure exponential curve they all wake up again in the same second, hit the service together and knock it over again. Jitter spreads each retry randomly across its window so the retries trickle in instead of arriving as a wave. It is one line in the delay function.
Stakes if we pick wrong: a recovering dependency gets re-flattened by our own synchronized retry storm, and the outage lasts longer than it needed to.
Recommendation: A because full jitter is the standard remedy for synchronized retries and costs one random call inside a function that is already being written. [Layer 1]
Completeness: A=10/10, B=7/10
Pros / cons:
A) Full jitter (recommended) (human: ~30 min incl. test / CC: ~3 min)
  ✅ Spreads retries uniformly across the window, so a recovering dependency sees a trickle, not a wave
  ✅ One expression in the delay function; the unit test seeds the RNG and asserts the range
  ❌ Individual retry timing is no longer exactly predictable from the attempt number alone
B) No jitter, deterministic exponential (human: ~0 / CC: ~0)
  ✅ Retry timing is exactly predictable, which makes log reading trivial
  ✅ Nothing extra to write or test
  ❌ Every job that failed together retries together, recreating the overload that caused the failure
Net: predictable timestamps in logs versus not DDoSing your own dependencies after an outage.

options.label: Full jitter (recommended)
options.description: Delay = random(0, min(cap, base * 2^attempt)). Unit test seeds the RNG and asserts the delay stays within [0, bound]. Completeness 10/10. Effort human ~30 min / CC ~3 min. R5b (cap) and R5c (exhaustion) stay pending and are asked next.

options.label: No jitter
options.description: Delay = base * 2^attempt, deterministic. Completeness 7/10. Effort none. R5b and R5c stay pending and are asked next.
